danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Tidligt i 1806 vendte Nikolaj Rostov hjem på orlov. Denisov var på vej hjem til Voronezj, og Rostov overtalte ham til at rejse med til Moskva og bo hos dem dér. Da de mødte en kammerat på den næstsidste poststation før Moskva, havde Denisov drukket tre flasker vin med ham, og på trods af de rystende hjulspor på den snedækkede vej vågnede han ikke en eneste gang på turen til Moskva, men lå i bunden af slæden ved siden af Rostov, der blev mere og mere utålmodig, jo nærmere de kom Moskva.

»Hvor langt endnu? Hvor langt endnu? Åh, disse ulidelige gader, butikker, bagerskilte, gadelygter og slæder!« tænkte Rostov, da deres orlovspas var blevet godkendt ved byens port, og de var kørt ind i Moskva.
»Denisov! Vi er her! Han sover,« tilføjede han og lænede sig fremad med hele kroppen, som om han i den stilling kunne få slæden til at køre hurtigere.
Denisov svarede ikke.

»Dér er hjørnet ved krydset, hvor droschkekusken Zakhar har sin plads, og dér er Zakhar selv med den samme hest! Og dér er den lille butik, hvor vi plejede at købe honningkager! Kan du ikke skynde dig? Kom nu!«
»Hvilket hus er det?« spurgte kusken.
»Det dér, helt nede for enden, det store hus. Kan du ikke se det? Det er vores hus,« sagde Rostov. »Selvfølgelig er det vores hus! Denisov, Denisov! Vi er næsten fremme!«
Denisov løftede hovedet, hostede og svarede ikke.
»Dmitrij,« sagde Rostov til sin tjener på bukken, »det er vel lys i vores hus, ikke?«
»Jo, herre, og der er lys i Deres fars arbejdsværelse.«

»Så er de ikke gået i seng endnu? Hvad tror du? Husk nu at finde min nye frakke frem,« tilføjede Rostov og mærkede på sit nye overskæg. »Kør nu! Skynd dig!« råbte han til kusken. »Vågn nu op, Vasja!« fortsatte han henvendt til Denisov, hvis hoved igen nikkede. »Kom nu, kør! Du skal få tre rubler til brændevin — kør nu!« råbte Rostov, da slæden kun var tre huse fra hans dør. Han syntes, hestene slet ikke rørte sig. Endelig drejede slæden til højre, standsede ved en indgang, og Rostov så den velkendte gamle gesims med et stykke puds slået af, trappen og stolpen ved fortovet. Han sprang ud, før slæden standsede, og løb ind i forhallen. Huset stod koldt og stille, som om det var ganske ligegyldigt med, hvem der var kommet. Der var ingen i forhallen. »Åh, Gud! Er alle i orden?« tænkte han og standsede et øjeblik med bankende hjerte, for straks efter at sætte i løb gennem forhallen og op ad de buede, velkendte trappetrins slidte trin. Det gamle velkendte dørhåndtag, som altid ærgrede grevinden, når det ikke var ordentligt pudset, drejede lige så løst som altid. Et ensomt tællelys brændte i forværelset.

Gamle Mikhael sov på kisten. Prokofij, lakajen, der var så stærk, at han kunne løfte bagenden af en karet alene, sad og flettede hjemmesko af stofkanter. Han så op, da døren gik op, og hans udtryk af søvnig ligegyldighed forvandledes pludselig til henrykt forbløffelse.

»Herregud! Den unge greve!« råbte han og genkendte sin unge herre. »Kan det virkelig passe? Min skat!« Og Prokofij, skælvende af begejstring, styrtede hen mod stuedøren, sandsynligvis for at melde ham, men ombestemte sig, vendte tilbage og bøjede sig ned for at kysse den unge mands skulder.
»Alle vel?« spurgte Rostov og trak sin arm til sig.
»Ja, Gud ske lov! Ja! De har lige spist til aften. Lad mig se på Dem, Deres excellence.«
»Er alt fuldstændig i orden?«
»Herren være lovet, ja!«

Rostov, der fuldstændig havde glemt Denisov, trak sin pelsfrakke af, da han ikke ville lade nogen komme ham i forkøbet, og løb på tåspidserne gennem den store mørke balsal. Alt var som før: de samme gamle spilleborde og den samme lysekrone med sit overtræk; men nogen havde allerede set den unge herre, og inden han nåede frem til dagligstuen, fløj noget ud fra en sidedør som en tornado og begyndte at kramme og kysse ham. Endnu et væsen af samme slags sprang ud fra en anden dør og et tredje; mere kramen, flere kys, flere udbrud og glædestårer. Han kunne ikke skelne, hvem der var Papa, hvem der var Natasja, og hvem der var Petja. Alle råbte, talte og kyssede ham på én gang. Kun hans mor var der ikke, bemærkede han.
»Og jeg vidste ikke ... Nikolaj ... min elskede! ...«
»Her er han ... vores egen ... Kolja, kære dreng ... Hvor han har forandret sig! ... Hvor er lysene? ... Te! ...«
* Kolja er kælenavn for Nikolaj.
»Og mig, kys mig!«
»Elskede ... og mig!«
Sonja, Natasja, Petja, Anna Mikhajlovna, Vera og den gamle greve krammede ham alle, og tjenestefolkene, mænd som piger, strømmede ind i stuen med udbrud og udråb.
Petja klamrede sig til hans ben og blev ved med at råbe: »Og mig også!«
Natasja trak ham ned mod sig og dækkede hans ansigt med kys, mens hun holdt ham fast i frakkeskødet, og sprang så fra ham og dansede op og ned på stedet som en killingeged og hylede gennemtrængende.
Rundt om var kærlige øjne, der glinsede af glædestårer, og overalt søgte læber et kys.

Sonja, helt rosenrød, klamrede sig også til hans arm og strålede af lykke, mens hun ivrigt søgte hans blik og ventede på det øjekast, hun længtes efter. Sonja var nu seksten og meget smuk, især i dette øjeblik af lykkelig, henrykt ophidselse. Hun så på ham uden at tage øjnene fra ham, smilende og tilbageholdende åndedrættet. Han sendte hende et taknemligt blik, men ventede stadig og ledte efter nogen. Den gamle grevinde var endnu ikke kommet. Men nu hørtes skridt ved døren, skridt så hurtige, at det næppe kunne være hans mor.

Alligevel var det hende, klædt i en ny kjole, han ikke kendte, syet siden han rejste. Alle de andre slap ham, og han løb hen til hende. Da de mødtes, faldt hun om på hans bryst og hulkede. Hun kunne ikke løfte ansigtet, men pressede det blot mod den kolde besnøring på hans husarjakke. Denisov, som var kommet ubemærket ind i stuen, stod der og tørrede sine øjne.
»Vasilij Denisov, Deres søns ven,« sagde han og præsenterede sig for greven, der så spørgende på ham.
»De er hjertelig velkommen! Jeg ved, jeg ved,« sagde greven og kyssede og omfavnede Denisov. »Nikolaj skrev til os ... Natasja, Vera, se! Her er Denisov!«
De samme lykkelige, henrykte ansigter vendte sig mod Denisovs strittende skikkelse.

»Kære Denisov!« skreg Natasja, ude af sig selv af henrykkelse, og sprang hen til ham, slog armene om ham og kyssede ham. Denne eskapade bragte alle i forlegenhed. Denisov rødmede også, men smilede og tog Natasjas hånd og kyssede den.
Denisov blev vist op til det værelse, der var gjort klar til ham, og hele familien Rostov samlede sig om Nikolaj i dagligstuen.

Den gamle grevinde, som ikke slap hans hånd og kyssede den hvert øjeblik, sad ved hans side; resten stod i klynge rundt om ham og fulgte enhver bevægelse, hvert ord, hvert blik med lykkeligt beundrende øjne. Hans bror og søstre kæmpede om pladserne nærmest ham og skændtes om, hvem der skulle bringe ham te, lommetørklæde og pibe.

Rostov var meget lykkelig over den kærlighed, de viste ham; men det første øjeblik af gensynet havde været så saligt, at hans nuværende glæde syntes utilstrækkelig, og han blev ved med at forvente noget mere, mere og endnu mere.
Næste morgen, efter rejsens strabadser, sov de rejsende til klokken ti.

I værelset ved siden af deres soveværelse var der et virvar af sabler, tasker, sabeltasker, åbne kufferter og beskidte støvler. To nypudsede par med sporer var netop stillet op ad væggen. Tjenerne bar vandkander og fade ind, varmt vand til barbering og nypudsede klæder. Der lugtede af mand og tobak.
»Hej, Grisja — min pibe!« lød Vasilij Denisovs hæse stemme. »Vostov, stå op!«
Rostov, der gned sine øjne, som var klistret sammen, løftede sit uredte hoved fra den varme pude.
»Er det sent?«

»Sent! Klokken er næsten ti,« svarede Natasjas stemme. En raslen af stivede underskørter og hvisken og latter af pigestemmer lød fra det tilstødende værelse. Døren blev åbnet på klem, og man skimtede noget blåt, bånd, sort hår og muntre ansigter. Det var Natasja, Sonja og Petja, der var kommet for at se, om de var stået op.
»Nikolaj! Stå op!« lød Natasjas stemme igen ved døren.
»Straks!«

Imens havde Petja fundet og bemægtiget sig sablerne i det ydre værelse med den begejstring, drenge føler ved synet af en militær storebror, og idet han glemte, at det var upassende for pigerne at se mænd i undertøj, åbnede han soveværelsesdøren.
»Er det din sabel?« råbte han.

Pigerne sprang til side. Denisov gemte sine hårede ben under tæppet og så med forskrækket ansigt på sin kammerat om hjælp. Døren, der havde lukket Petja ind, smækkede i igen. Latter lød fra den anden side.
»Nikolaj! Kom ud i din slobrok!« sagde Natasjas stemme.
»Er det din sabel?« spurgte Petja. »Eller er den din?« sagde han henvendt til den sortmoustacherede Denisov med servil ærbødighed.

Rostov trak hastigt noget på fødderne, tog sin slobrok på og gik ud. Natasja havde taget den ene sporebesatte støvle på og var ved at få foden ned i den anden. Sonja, da han kom ind, snurrede rundt om sig selv og var ved at svinge sine skørter ud som en ballon og sætte sig ned. De var klædt ens i nye lyseblå kjoler, begge friske, rosenrøde og strålende. Sonja løb bort, men Natasja tog sin bror under armen og førte ham ind i dagligstuen, hvor de begyndte at snakke. De gav næppe hinanden tid til at stille spørgsmål og give svar om tusind små ting, som ikke kunne interessere andre end dem selv. Natasja lo af hvert ord, han sagde, eller som hun selv sagde, ikke fordi det, de talte om, var morsomt, men fordi hun var lykkelig og ude af stand til at styre sin glæde, der udtrykte sig i latter.
»Åh, hvor dejligt, hvor vidunderligt!« sagde hun til alting.

Rostov følte, at under de varme stråler af kærlighed smeltede det barnlige smil, der ikke en eneste gang havde vist sig på hans ansigt, siden han forlod hjemmet, nu for første gang efter atten måneder atter frem og oplyste hans sjæl og hans ansigt.

»Nej, men hør nu,« sagde hun, »nu er du jo helt en rigtig mand, ikke? Jeg er forfærdelig glad for, at du er min bror.« Hun rørte ved hans overskæg. »Jeg vil gerne vide, hvordan I mænd er. Er I ligesom os? Nej?«
»Hvorfor løb Sonja sin vej?« spurgte Rostov.
»Åh ja! Det er en lang historie! Hvordan vil du tiltale hende — du eller De?«
»Som det falder sig,« sagde Rostov.

»Nej, sig De til hende, det er bedst! Det skal jeg nok fortælle dig om en anden gang. Nej, jeg fortæller det nu. Du ved, Sonja er min allerbedste veninde. Sådan en ven, at jeg har brændt min arm for hendes skyld. Se her!«
Hun trak sit muslinærme op og viste ham et rødt ar på sin lange, slanke, fine arm, højt over albuen på det sted, der er dækket selv af en balkjole.
»Det her brændte jeg for at bevise min kærlighed til hende. Jeg varmede simpelthen en lineal i ilden og trykkede den mod armen!«

Siddende i sofaen med de små puder på armlænene, i det, der plejede at være hans gamle skolestue, og seende ind i Natasjas vildt strålende øjne, genindtrådte Rostov i den verden af hjem og barndom, som ikke betød noget for nogen anden, men som gav ham nogle af livets skønneste glæder; og det at brænde sin arm med en lineal som bevis på kærlighed forekom ham ikke meningsløst — han forstod det og blev ikke forbavset.
»Nå, er det det hele?« spurgte han.

»Vi er sådan nogle veninder, sådan nogle veninder! Alt det med linealen var bare pjat, men vi er veninder for evigt. Hvis hun elsker nogen, gør hun det for livet, men sådan er jeg ikke — jeg glemmer hurtigt.«
»Nå, og hvad så?«
»Jo, hun elsker mig og dig på den måde.«
Natasja rødmede pludselig.

»Jamen, husker du — før du rejste? ... Jo altså, hun siger, at du skal glemme alt det der ... Hun siger: 'Jeg vil altid elske ham, men lad ham være fri.' Er det ikke smukt og ædelt? Jo, meget ædelt? Er det ikke?« spurgte Natasja så alvorligt og ophidset, at det var tydeligt, at det, hun nu sagde, var noget, hun før havde talt om under tårer.
Rostov blev eftertænksom.
»Jeg tager aldrig mine ord tilbage,« sagde han. »Desuden er Sonja så charmerende, at kun en tåbe ville give afkald på en sådan lykke.«

»Nej, nej!« udbrød Natasja, »hun og jeg har allerede drøftet det. Vi vidste, du ville sige sådan. Men det dur ikke, for ser du — hvis du siger det, hvis du betragter dig som bundet af dit løfte, vil det se ud, som om hun ikke havde ment det alvorligt. Det bliver som om du gifter dig med hende, fordi du er nødt til det, og det ville slet ikke gå.«

Rostov indså, at de havde tænkt det grundigt igennem. Sonja havde allerede dagen før slået ham med sin skønhed. I dag, da han havde fået et glimt af hende, syntes hun endnu smukkere. Hun var en charmerende pige på seksten, tydeligvis lidenskabeligt forelsket i ham (det tvivlede han ikke et øjeblik på). Hvorfor skulle han ikke elske hende nu og endda gifte sig med hende, tænkte Rostov, men netop nu lå der så mange andre glæder og interesser foran ham! »Ja, de har truffet en klog beslutning,« tænkte han, »jeg må forblive fri.«
»Nå, det er udmærket,« sagde han. »Vi taler om det senere. Åh, hvor er jeg glad for at have dig!«
»Nå, og er du stadig tro mod Boris?« fortsatte han.
»Åh, sikke noget vrøvl!« udbrød Natasja leende. »Jeg tænker hverken på ham eller nogen anden, og det vil jeg heller ikke.«
»Javel! Hvad går du så rundt og laver?«
»Nu?« gentog Natasja, og et lykkeligt smil oplyste hendes ansigt. »Har du set Duport?«
»Nej.«
»Ikke set Duport — den berømte danser? Nå, så kan du heller ikke forstå det. Det er dét, jeg går og laver.«
Natasja svingede armene i en bue, holdt skørterne ud som dansere gør det, løb et par skridt baglæns, vendte sig, slog et hop, samlede sine små fødder og gik et par skridt helt oppe på tåspidserne.
»Se, jeg står! Se!« sagde hun, men kunne ikke holde sig på tåspidserne længere. »Så det er dét, jeg laver! Jeg gifter mig aldrig med nogen, men bliver danserinde. Men sig det ikke til nogen.«
Rostov lo så højt og muntert, at Denisov i sit soveværelse blev misundelig, og Natasja ikke kunne lade være med at stemme i.
»Nej, men er det ikke dejligt?« blev hun ved med at sige.
»Dejligt! Og så vil du altså ikke giftes med Boris?«
Natasja blussede op. »Jeg vil ikke giftes med nogen. Og det skal jeg nok fortælle ham, når jeg ser ham!«
»Jøsses!« sagde Rostov.
»Men alt det er jo vrøvl,« plaprede Natasja videre. »Og er Denisov flink?« spurgte hun.
»Ja, bestemt!«
»Nå, så farvel: gå hen og klæd dig om. Er han meget skræmmende, Denisov?«
»Hvorfor skræmmende?« spurgte Nikolaj. »Nej, Vasja er en storartet fyr.«
»Du kalder ham Vasja? Det er sjovt! Og er han meget flink?«
»Meget.«
»Nå, skynd dig så. Vi spiser morgenmad sammen alle.«

Og Natasja rejste sig og gik ud af stuen på tåspidserne som en balletdanserinde, men med det smil, kun lykkelige femtenårige piger kan smile. Da Rostov mødte Sonja i dagligstuen, rødmede han. Han vidste ikke, hvordan han skulle opføre sig over for hende. Aftenen før, i det første lykkelige gensynsøjeblik, havde de kysset hinanden, men i dag følte de, at det ikke kunne lade sig gøre; han fornemmede, at alle — hans mor, hans søstre — så spørgende på ham og ventede på at se, hvordan han ville opføre sig over for hende. Han kyssede hendes hånd og sagde De til hende i stedet for du. Men deres øjne mødtes og sagde du, og de udvekslede ømme kys. Hendes blik bad ham tilgive hende, at hun gennem Natasja havde vovet at minde ham om hans løfte, og takkede ham derefter for hans kærlighed. Hans blik takkede hende for at have givet ham hans frihed og fortalte hende, at han på den ene eller anden måde aldrig ville ophøre med at elske hende, for det var umuligt.
»Hvor mærkeligt det er,« sagde Vera, der udvalgte et øjeblik, da alle var tavse, »at Sonja og Nikolaj nu siger De til hinanden og mødes som fremmede.«

Veras bemærkning var rigtig, som hendes bemærkninger altid var, men som de fleste af hendes observationer fik den alle til at føle sig ilde til mode — ikke blot Sonja, Nikolaj og Natasja, men selv den gamle grevinde, der frygtede dette kærlighedsforhold, som kunne hindre Nikolaj i at gøre et strålende parti, og hun rødmede som en ung pige.

Denisov dukkede til Rostovs overraskelse op i dagligstuen med pomadiseret hår, parfumeret og i en ny uniform, og så lige så pæn ud, som når han skulle i slag, og han var langt mere elskværdig over for damerne og herrerne, end Rostov nogensinde ville have forventet.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Early in 1806, Nicholas Rostov returned home on leave. Denisov was heading to Voronezh, and Rostov convinced him to travel together as far as Moscow and stay with him there. At the last post station before Moscow, Denisov had drunk three bottles of wine with a fellow officer and, despite the jolting ride over the rutted, snow-covered road, slept the entire way, lying at the bottom of the sleigh beside Rostov, who grew more and more impatient as they neared the city.

"How much farther? How much longer? These unbearable streets, shops, bakery signs, street lamps, and sleighs!" Rostov thought, after their travel permits had been checked at the city gate and they had entered Moscow.
"Denisov! We're here! He's asleep," he added, leaning his whole body forward as if that might somehow make the sleigh go faster.
Denisov didn't answer.

"There's the corner where the cabman Zakhar has his stand — and there's Zakhar himself, with the same old horse! And there's the little shop where we used to buy gingerbread! Can't you go faster? Come on!"
"Which house?" asked the driver.
"That one, right at the end, the big one. Can't you see? That's our house," said Rostov. "Of course it's our house! Denisov, Denisov! We're almost there!"
Denisov lifted his head, coughed, and said nothing.
"Dmitri," said Rostov to his servant on the box, "those lights are in our house, aren't they?"
"Yes, sir, and there's a light on in your father's study."

"So they haven't gone to bed yet! Good. And don't forget to put out my new coat," added Rostov, fingering his new mustache. "Now hurry up," he shouted to the driver. "Wake up, Vaska!" he said, turning to Denisov, whose head was nodding again. "Come on, get moving! I'll give you three rubles for vodka — just go!" Rostov shouted when the sleigh was only three houses from his door. It felt as though the horses had stopped moving entirely. At last the sleigh turned right, pulled up at an entrance, and Rostov looked up to see the old familiar cornice with its bit of chipped plaster, the porch, and the post beside the pavement. He leaped out before the sleigh had stopped and ran into the hall. The house was cold and quiet, as if it didn't care who had come to it. There was no one in the hall. "Oh God! Is everyone all right?" he thought, pausing for a moment with a sinking heart, then immediately running through the hall and up the worn, familiar staircase. The old door handle — the one that always annoyed the countess when it wasn't properly cleaned — turned as loosely as ever. A single tallow candle burned in the anteroom.

Old Mikhail was asleep on the chest. Prokofy the footman, who was so strong he could lift the back of a carriage by himself, sat braiding slippers from cloth scraps. He looked up when the door opened, and his expression of sleepy indifference instantly transformed into delighted amazement.

"Good heavens! The young count!" he cried, recognizing his young master. "Can it be? My dear boy!" And Prokofy, trembling with excitement, rushed toward the drawing room door — probably to announce him — but then changed his mind, came back, and bent down to kiss the young man's shoulder.
"Everyone well?" asked Rostov, pulling his arm away.
"Yes, thank God! Yes! They've just finished supper. Let me look at you, your excellency."
"Everything's really all right?"
"Yes, thank the Lord!"

Rostov, who had completely forgotten about Denisov and not wanting anyone to get there before him, threw off his fur coat and ran on tiptoe through the large, dark ballroom. Everything was the same: the same old card tables, the same chandelier with its dust cover. But someone had already spotted the young master, and before he reached the drawing room, something burst from a side door like a whirlwind and started hugging and kissing him. Then another creature of the same kind flew out from a second door, and a third — more hugging, more kissing, more shouts and tears of joy. He couldn't tell who was Papa, who was Natasha, and who was Petya. Everyone shouted, talked, and kissed him all at once. Only his mother was not among them, he noticed.
"I didn't know... Nicholas... My darling!..."
"Here he is... our own boy... Kolya, sweetheart... How he's changed!... Where are the candles?... Tea!..."
* Kolya is the familiar form of Nicholas.
"And me — kiss me!"
"Darling... and me!"
Sonya, Natasha, Petya, Anna Mikhaylovna, Vera, and the old count were all hugging him, while the servants — men and women alike — crowded into the room, exclaiming and gasping.
Petya clung to his legs, shouting, "And me too!"
Natasha, after pulling him down toward her and covering his face with kisses while gripping the hem of his coat, sprang away and began prancing in place like a goat, letting out a piercing shriek.
All around him were loving eyes glistening with tears of joy, and everywhere were lips seeking a kiss.

Sonya too, her face flushed pink, clung to his arm and gazed at him, radiant with happiness, eagerly waiting for the look she longed for. She was sixteen now and very pretty, especially at this moment of joyful, rapturous excitement. She stared at him without blinking, smiling and holding her breath. He gave her a grateful look but was still searching for someone. The old countess hadn't come yet. Then footsteps were heard at the door — footsteps so rapid they could hardly be his mother's.

Yet it was her, wearing a new dress he didn't recognize, made after he had left. Everyone else let go of him, and he ran to her. When they met, she fell against his chest, sobbing. She couldn't lift her face — she just pressed it against the cold braiding of his hussar jacket. Denisov, who had entered the room unnoticed, stood there and wiped his eyes at the sight.
"Vasili Denisov, your son's friend," he said, introducing himself to the count, who was looking at him questioningly.
"Welcome! Most welcome! I know, I know," said the count, kissing and embracing Denisov. "Nicholas wrote us about you... Natasha, Vera — look! Here is Denisov!"
The same happy, glowing faces turned toward Denisov's shaggy figure.

"Dear Denisov!" screamed Natasha, beside herself with joy, springing toward him, throwing her arms around him, and kissing him. This display made everyone feel a bit awkward. Denisov blushed too, but smiled, took Natasha's hand, and kissed it.
Denisov was shown to his room, and the Rostovs all gathered around Nicholas in the sitting room.

The old countess, refusing to let go of his hand and kissing it every other moment, sat beside him. The rest crowded around, watching his every movement, word, and expression, never taking their adoring eyes off him. His brother and sisters jostled for the spots closest to him and argued over who would bring him his tea, his handkerchief, his pipe.

Rostov was deeply happy in the love they showed him, but the first moment of reunion had been so perfect that now his joy seemed insufficient, and he kept expecting something more — more and still more.
The next morning, after the fatigue of their journey, the travelers slept until ten o'clock.

In the room next to their bedroom lay a jumble of sabers, satchels, sword belts, open trunks, and dirty boots. Two freshly cleaned pairs with spurs had just been set against the wall. Servants brought in pitchers and basins, hot water for shaving, and well-brushed clothes. The room smelled of men and tobacco.
"Hey, Grishka — my pipe!" came Denisov's husky voice. "Rostov, get up!"
Rostov, rubbing his eyes, which seemed glued shut, lifted his tousled head from the warm pillow.
"Is it late?"

"Late! It's nearly ten o'clock," answered Natasha's voice. A rustle of starched petticoats and the whispering and laughter of girls came from the next room. The door cracked open and there was a glimpse of something blue — ribbons, dark hair, and cheerful faces. It was Natasha, Sonya, and Petya, who had come to check if they were up yet.
"Nicholas! Get up!" Natasha's voice came again at the door.
"Coming!"

Meanwhile Petya, who had found the sabers in the outer room, seized them with a boy's natural delight at anything military. Forgetting that it wasn't proper for the girls to see men undressed, he threw open the bedroom door.
"Is this your saber?" he shouted.

The girls jumped aside. Denisov hid his hairy legs under the blanket and looked with a panicked face at his comrade for help. The door, having let Petya in, closed again. Laughter erupted from behind it.
"Nicholas! Come out in your dressing gown!" called Natasha's voice.
"Is this your saber?" asked Petya. "Or is it yours?" he added, turning to the dark-mustached Denisov with exaggerated respect.

Rostov hurriedly pulled on something for his feet, threw on his dressing gown, and came out. Natasha had put on one spurred boot and was trying to get her foot into the other. Sonya was twirling around, about to puff out her skirts like a balloon and sit down. They were both wearing identical new pale-blue dresses, and both looked fresh, rosy, and bright. Sonya ran off, but Natasha took her brother's arm and led him to the sitting room, where they started talking. They barely gave each other time to ask questions and get answers about a thousand small things that could only matter to the two of them. Natasha laughed at everything he said and everything she said — not because any of it was funny, but because she was happy and couldn't contain her joy, which came out as laughter.
"Oh, how lovely! How wonderful!" she said to everything.

Rostov felt that under the influence of the warm glow of love, the childlike smile that had not appeared on his face once since he left home now returned for the first time in eighteen months, brightening both his soul and his face.
"No, but listen," she said, "you're really a grown man now, aren't you? I'm so glad you're my brother." She touched his mustache. "I want to know what you men are like. Are you the same as us? No?"
"Why did Sonya run away?" asked Rostov.
"Oh, that's a whole long story! How are you going to talk to her — formally or informally?"
"However it happens," said Rostov.
"No, use the formal 'you,' please! I'll tell you all about it another time. Actually, I'll tell you now. You know Sonya is my dearest friend. Such a close friend that I burned my arm for her. Look!"
She pushed up her muslin sleeve and showed him a red scar on her long, slender arm, high above the elbow — a spot normally covered even by a ball gown.
"I burned this to prove my love for her. I just heated a ruler over a candle and pressed it right there!"

Sitting on the sofa with the little cushions on its arms, in what had been his old schoolroom, looking into Natasha's wildly bright eyes, Rostov re-entered that world of home and childhood that meant nothing to anyone else but gave him some of the greatest joys of his life. Burning one's arm with a ruler to prove love didn't seem senseless to him — he understood it and wasn't surprised by it at all.
"And that's all?" he asked.

"We're such friends, such close friends! All that ruler business was just silliness, but we're friends forever. When she loves someone, she does it for life — but I'm not like that. I forget quickly."
"So what then?"
"She loves me, and she loves you the same way."
Natasha suddenly blushed.

"She says you should forget all about what happened before you left.... She says, 'I will always love him, but let him be free.' Isn't that beautiful and noble? Yes, really noble — isn't it?" asked Natasha, so seriously and passionately that it was clear she had discussed this before, with tears.
Rostov grew thoughtful.
"I never go back on my word," he said. "Besides, Sonya is so lovely that only a fool would give up such happiness."

"No, no!" cried Natasha. "She and I have already talked about this. We knew you'd say that. But it won't work, because if you say it like that — if you act like you're bound by your promise — then it seems as though she wasn't being sincere. It would make it look like you're marrying her out of obligation, and that's no good at all."

Rostov saw that they had thought this through carefully. Sonya had already struck him with her beauty the day before. Today, having caught a glimpse of her, she seemed even lovelier. She was a charming sixteen-year-old girl, obviously passionately in love with him — he didn't doubt that for a moment. Why shouldn't he love her now, and even marry her? But at the moment, there were so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him! "Yes, they've made a wise decision," he thought. "I should stay free."
"Well then, that's perfect," he said. "We'll talk about it later. Oh, how glad I am to have you!"
"So — are you still faithful to Boris?" he continued.
"Oh, what nonsense!" cried Natasha, laughing. "I don't think about him or anyone else, and I don't want any of that."
"Really! So what are you up to these days?"
"These days?" repeated Natasha, and a happy smile lit up her face. "Have you seen Duport?"
"No."
"You haven't seen Duport — the famous dancer? Well then, you won't understand. That's what I'm up to."

Curving her arms and holding out her skirts like a ballerina, Natasha backed up a few steps, spun around, performed a little jump, clicked her feet sharply together, and rose up on the very tips of her toes.
"See? I'm standing! See!" she said, but couldn't hold herself on her toes any longer. "So that's what I'm doing! I'll never marry anyone — I'm going to be a dancer. But don't tell anyone."
Rostov laughed so loudly and joyfully that Denisov in the bedroom felt a pang of envy, and Natasha couldn't help joining in.
"Don't you think it's wonderful?" she kept repeating.
"Wonderful! And so you don't want to marry Boris anymore?"
Natasha flared up. "I don't want to marry anyone. And I'll tell him so myself when I see him!"
"Goodness!" said Rostov.
"But that's all silly," Natasha chattered on. "Is Denisov nice?" she asked.
"Very nice."
"Well then — goodbye. Go get dressed. Is he very scary, Denisov?"
"Why scary?" asked Nicholas. "No, Vaska is a wonderful fellow."
"You call him Vaska? That's funny! Is he really nice?"
"Very."
"All right then, hurry up. We'll all have breakfast together."

And Natasha rose and tiptoed out of the room like a ballerina, but with the kind of smile that only happy fifteen-year-old girls can manage. When Rostov met Sonya in the drawing room, he blushed. He didn't know how to behave around her. The night before, in the first joyful moment of reunion, they had kissed. But today that felt impossible. He sensed that everyone — his mother, his sisters, all of them — was watching him, waiting to see how he would act with her. He kissed her hand and addressed her formally. But their eyes met and spoke intimately, exchanging tender, silent kisses. Her gaze asked forgiveness for having dared, through Natasha, to remind him of his promise — and thanked him for his love. His gaze thanked her for offering him his freedom and told her that one way or another, he would never stop loving her, because that would be impossible.
"How strange," said Vera, choosing a moment when everyone was silent, "that Sonya and Nicholas now address each other formally and act like strangers."

Vera's observation was accurate, as her remarks always were. But like most of her comments, it made everyone uncomfortable — not just Sonya, Nicholas, and Natasha, but even the old countess, who dreaded this love affair that might prevent Nicholas from making a brilliant match. She blushed like a young girl.

Denisov, to Rostov's surprise, appeared in the drawing room with pomaded hair, wearing cologne and a new uniform, looking as sharp as he made himself before going into battle. He was more charming with the ladies and gentlemen than Rostov had ever seen him.
